newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers keep up oil blockade as talks fail.
newsitem.headline: French truckers keep up oil blockade as talks fail.

text.p: French truckers targeted the oil industry at the start of a second week on Monday after talks to end an eight-day-old haulage strike broke down in deadlock.
Oil companies said parked lorries were blocking access to several refineries and depots as more petrol stations ran short of fuel in the worst affected southern and northern regions.

Among the refineries still behind barriers on Monday were Royal Dutch/Shell's Mediterranean oil and complex at Berre, near Marseille, Total's Dunkirk refinery in the north and Elf Aquitaine's Donges refinery in the west, industry sources said.
Problems in getting hold of petrol appeared to take hold mainly in the south and north of the country. But there was no serious talk of widespread shortages at the pumps.
However, oil company officials warned privately it would become increasingly difficult to guarantee supplies if the strike lasted more than a few days.
Not only was the strike hitting fuel depots directly, but those petrol tankers which were on the road were having problems getting round the blockades on major highways, they said.
"I think people are already filling up their tanks, and if this continues we should not rule out some problems in a week," said one official at a top oil company, asking not to be named.
Refinery output is currently intact but may have to be trimmed if the strike lasts a week, a refinery official said.
In the southern cities of Aix-en-Provence, Marseille and Toulon about half the petrol forecourts were closed and motorists faced delays of about an hour at supermarket pumps.
Truckers who want higher pay, shorter hours and early retirement are targeting fuel logistics in a cat-and-mouse game with the oil industry to apply economic pressure.
Several distribution depots were blocked on Monday, although it was impossible to obtain an exact number as several oil firms worried about drawing attention to depots that were now running.

"It is not a secret, but it is not information we give out," said one oil company spokeswoman, asked how many fuel depots the company operated in France. "Overall the situation is difficult today," she added, however.

In specific disruption, Elf's Donges refinery was operating normally but its distribution centres for "white" and "black" oil -- essentially the difference between transportation fuel and heavy fuel for power stations and industry -- were sealed off.
At Shell's Berre refinery truckers continued to block access to loading ramps for petrol, diesel and plastic-type chemicals.
The situation at Elf's Feyzin refinery near Lyon was less clear after the plant had to cope with blockades last week. One industry source said access to the plant was "up and down".
The capital Paris was not affected.
Oil companies said they were frantically juggling delivery plans and schedules to try to keep the main network supplied.
"It is clear there are some parts that are not well supplied, where we are seeing some breaks, but we don't have big shortages yet. Several depots are still going," said one source.
Truck unions were not immediately available for comment on the fuel disruption.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe, saying he was monitoring the situation "hour-by-hour", called on Monday for talks to resume.
-- Tim Hepher, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
